analysis.one_liner: Removes dollar caps on damages for victims of intentional job discrimination.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in May 1992, but it never got a floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1991 Civil Rights Act let workers win money damages for intentional job discrimination, but it capped how much could be awarded for personal losses and punitive damages. This bill would strike those caps, so a jury could award whatever compensation it found warranted, and would guarantee any party the right to a jury trial. It cleared the Senate labor committee and sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ran out.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are intentionally discriminated against by their employers — including women, religious minorities, and people with disabilities, whose claims the 1991 law capped at modest dollar limits — would be able to recover full compensation, including punitive damages, as determined by a jury.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the limits the Civil Rights Act of 1991 placed on damages for financial losses, personal losses, and punitive damages in intentional employment discrimination cases [S2] [S3].
Makes remedies equal across all victims of intentional discrimination, as its title states, so that caps no longer fall unevenly on workers depending on which type of discrimination they faced [S3].
Guarantees any party in a damages case the right to demand a jury trial [S3].
The bill was introduced with 37 cosponsors, including 5 Republicans, and was reported out of committee without amendment favorably [S4] [S5] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for intentional discrimination would face uncapped compensatory and punitive awards instead of the fixed limits in current law, and would lose the predictability those caps provided.

drawbacks.text: The caps being struck were created by section 1977A as added by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, meaning the bill would undo a limit deliberately written into that law [S3].

Without caps, employers found liable would face uncapped compensatory and punitive damages, which supporters of the 1991 limits argued gives employers a reason to settle quickly but critics a reason to fear unpredictable jury awards and higher litigation costs [S2] [S3].
Larger awards flow to the workers with the strongest cases rather than spreading benefits broadly; most workers never bring such claims at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: it would let juries fully compensate proven victims of intentional discrimination instead of capping them at fixed dollar limits, and it had genuine bipartisan support. The honest cost is that uncapped punitive damages make outcomes less predictable for employers and could push them toward more cautious, costlier legal behavior. The caps were a deliberate part of the 1991 compromise, so removing them would have reopened a settled bargain — a fair objection, though one that weighs the certainty of employers against compensation for workers who were actually discriminated against.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar in May 1992, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 26, 1991 by Senator Kennedy with 37 cosponsors, including 5 Republicans, and was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1] [S4] [S5].
On March 11, 1992 the committee ordered it reported favorably without amendment, and on May 21, 1992 Senator Kennedy reported it to the Senate with a written report, with additional views filed [S5].
The same day it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where a bill waits for the Senate to take it up [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred; the bill remained on the calendar until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing discrimination claims, who kept the damage caps as a shield limiting their liability; workers who face intentional discrimination gained nothing, since the caps remained in force.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who kept the damage caps

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through committee, and reported it to the Senate floor.

for.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over employment law
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment and reported it to the Senate.

for.name: 37 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors including 5 Republicans such as Sens. McConnell, Packwood, and Durenberger

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.role: Controls which calendar bills get floor time
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for a vote after it was placed on the calendar in May 1992.

against.name: Employer and business groups
against.role: Business coalitions that backed the damage caps in the 1991 civil rights compromise
against.what_they_did: Opposed reopening the Civil Rights Act of 1991 to lift the caps on damages, defending the limits negotiated to win that law's passage.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes at all: 5 of the 37 cosponsors were Republicans and the committee reported the bill favorably without amendment, but the Senate never took it up, so the partisan split on a final vote is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would remove the caps that limit what employers must pay workers they are found to have intentionally discriminated against. The industry's interest in keeping the caps runs against the workers seeking full compensation.

industries.industry: Employment discrimination plaintiffs and their attorneys
industries.note: Uncapped damages and a guaranteed jury-trial right would raise the value and viability of discrimination claims, and the lawyers who bring them would share in larger fee awards.
